==Problem==

Two lines with slopes <math>\dfrac{1}{2}</math> and <math>2</math> intersect at <math>(2,2)</math>. What is the area of the triangle enclosed by these two lines and the line <math>x+y=10  ?</math>

<math>\textbf{(A) } 4 \qquad\textbf{(B) } 4\sqrt{2} \qquad\textbf{(C) } 6 \qquad\textbf{(D) } 8 \qquad\textbf{(E) } 6\sqrt{2}</math>

==Solution 1==
Let's first work out the slope-intercept form of all three lines:
<imath>(x,y)=(2,2)</imath> and <imath>y=\frac{x}{2} + b</imath> implies <imath>2=\frac{2}{2} +b=> 2=1+b</imath> so <imath>b=1</imath>, while <imath>y=2x + c</imath> implies <imath>2= 2 \cdot 2+c=> 2=4+c</imath> so <imath>c=-2</imath>. Also, <imath>x+y=10</imath> implies <imath>y=-x+10</imath>. Thus the lines are <imath>y=\frac{x}{2} +1, y=2x-2,</imath> and <imath>y=-x+10</imath>. 
Now we find the intersection points between each of the lines with <imath>y=-x+10</imath>, which are <imath>(6,4)</imath> and <imath>(4,6)</imath>. Using the distance formula and then the Pythagorean Theorem, we see that we have an isosceles triangle with base <imath>2\sqrt{2}</imath> and height <imath>3\sqrt{2}</imath>, whose area is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(C) }6}</imath>.

==Solution 2==
Like in the other solutions, solve the systems of equations to see that the triangle's two other vertices are at <imath>(4, 6)</imath> and <imath>(6, 4)</imath>. Then apply Heron's Formula: the semi-perimeter will be <imath>s = \sqrt{2} + \sqrt{20}</imath>, so the area reduces nicely to a difference of squares, making it <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(C) }6}</imath>.

==Solution 3==
Like in the other solutions, we find, either using algebra or simply by drawing the lines on squared paper, that the three points of intersection are <imath>(2, 2)</imath>, <imath>(4, 6)</imath>, and <imath>(6, 4)</imath>. We can now draw the bounding square with vertices <imath>(2, 2)</imath>, <imath>(2, 6)</imath>, <imath>(6, 6)</imath> and <imath>(6, 2)</imath>, and deduce that the triangle's area is <imath>16-4-2-4=\boxed{\textbf{(C) }6}</imath>.

==Solution 4==
Like in other solutions, we find that the three points of intersection are  <imath>(2, 2)</imath>, <imath>(4, 6)</imath>, and <imath>(6, 4)</imath>. Using graph paper, we can see that this triangle has <imath>6</imath> boundary lattice points and <imath>4</imath> interior lattice points. By Pick's Theorem, the area is <imath>\frac62 + 4 - 1 = \boxed{\textbf{(C) }6}</imath>.

==Solution 5==
Like in other solutions, we find the three points of intersection. Label these <imath>A (2, 2)</imath>, <imath>B (4, 6)</imath>, and <imath>C (6, 4)</imath>. By the Pythagorean Theorem, <imath>AB = AC = 2\sqrt5</imath> and <imath>BC = 2\sqrt2</imath>. By the Law of Cosines,
<cmath>\cos A = \frac{(2\sqrt5)^2 + (2\sqrt5)^2 - (2\sqrt2)^2}{2 \cdot 2\sqrt5 \cdot 2\sqrt5} = \frac{20 + 20 - 8}{40} = \frac{32}{40} = \frac45</cmath>
Therefore, <imath>\sin A = \sqrt{1 - \cos^2 A} = \frac35</imath>, so the area is <imath>\frac12 bc \sin A = \frac12 \cdot 2\sqrt5 \cdot 2\sqrt5 \cdot \frac35 = \boxed{\textbf{(C) }6}</imath>.

==Solution 6==
Like in other solutions, we find that the three points of intersection are  <imath>(2, 2)</imath>, <imath>(4, 6)</imath>, and <imath>(6, 4)</imath>. The area of the triangle is half the absolute value of the determinant of the matrix determined by these points.
<cmath>
\frac12\begin{Vmatrix}
2&2&1\\
4&6&1\\
6&4&1\\
\end{Vmatrix} = \frac12|-12| = \frac12 \cdot 12 = \boxed{\textbf{(C) }6}</cmath>

==Solution 7==
Like in other solutions, we find the three points of intersection. Label these <imath>A (2, 2)</imath>, <imath>B (4, 6)</imath>, and <imath>C (6, 4)</imath>. Then vectors <imath>\overrightarrow{AB} = \langle 2, 4 \rangle</imath> and <imath>\overrightarrow{AC} = \langle 4, 2 \rangle</imath>. The area of the triangle is half the magnitude of the cross product of these two vectors.
<cmath>
\frac12\begin{Vmatrix}
i&j&k\\
2&4&0\\
4&2&0\\
\end{Vmatrix} = \frac12|-12k| = \frac12 \cdot 12 = \boxed{\textbf{(C) }6}</cmath>

==Solution 8==
Like in other solutions, we find that the three points of intersection are <imath>(2, 2)</imath>, <imath>(4, 6)</imath>, and <imath>(6, 4)</imath>. By the Pythagorean theorem, this is an isosceles triangle with base <imath>2\sqrt2</imath> and equal length <imath>2\sqrt5</imath>. The area of an isosceles triangle with base <imath>b</imath> and equal length <imath>l</imath> is <imath>\frac{b\sqrt{4l^2-b^2}}{4}</imath>. Plugging  in <imath>b = 2\sqrt2</imath> and <imath>l = 2\sqrt5</imath>,
<cmath>\frac{2\sqrt2 \cdot \sqrt{80-8}}{4} = \frac{\sqrt{576}}{4} = \frac{24}{4} = \boxed{\textbf{(C) }6}</cmath>

==Solution 9 (Trig) ==
Like in other solutions, we find the three points of intersection. Label these <imath>A (2, 2)</imath>, <imath>B (4, 6)</imath>, and <imath>C (6, 4)</imath>. By the Pythagorean Theorem, <imath>AB = AC = 2\sqrt5</imath> and <imath>BC = 2\sqrt2</imath>. By the Law of Cosines,
<cmath>\cos A = \frac{(2\sqrt5)^2 + (2\sqrt5)^2 - (2\sqrt2)^2}{2 \cdot 2\sqrt5 \cdot 2\sqrt5} = \frac{20 + 20 - 8}{40} = \frac{32}{40} = \frac45</cmath>
Therefore, <imath>\sin A = \sqrt{1 - \cos^2 A} = \frac35</imath>. By the extended Law of Sines,
<cmath>2R = \frac{a}{\sin A} = \frac{2\sqrt2}{\frac35} = \frac{10\sqrt2}{3}</cmath>
<cmath>R = \frac{5\sqrt2}{3}</cmath>
Then the area is <imath>\frac{abc}{4R} = \frac{2\sqrt2 \cdot 2\sqrt5^2}{4 \cdot \frac{5\sqrt2}{3}} = \boxed{\textbf{(C) }6}</imath>.

==Solution 10==
The area of a triangle formed by three lines,
<cmath>a_1x + a_2y + a_3 = 0</cmath>
<cmath>b_1x + b_2y + b_3 = 0</cmath>
<cmath>c_1x + c_2y + c_3 = 0</cmath>
is the absolute value of
<cmath>\frac12 \cdot \frac{1}{(b_1c_2-b_2c_1)(a_1c_2-a_2c_1)(a_1b_2-a_2b_1)} \cdot \begin{vmatrix}
a_1&a_2&a_3\\
b_1&b_2&b_3\\
c_1&c_2&c_3\\
\end{vmatrix}^2</cmath>
Plugging in the three lines,
<cmath>-x + 2y - 2 = 0</cmath>
<cmath>-2x + y + 2 = 0</cmath>
<cmath>x + y - 10 = 0</cmath>
the area is the absolute value of
<cmath>\frac12 \cdot \frac{1}{(-2-1)(-1-2)(-1+4)} \cdot \begin{vmatrix}
-1&2&-2\\
-2&1&2\\
1&1&-10\\
\end{vmatrix}^2 = \frac12 \cdot \frac{1}{27} \cdot 18^2 = \boxed{\textbf{(C) }6}</cmath>
Source: Orrick, Michael L. “THE AREA OF A TRIANGLE FORMED BY THREE LINES.” Pi Mu Epsilon Journal, vol. 7, no. 5, 1981, pp. 294–298. JSTOR, www.jstor.org/stable/24336991.

==Solution 11 (Heron's Formula) ==

Like in other solutions, we find that our triangle is isosceles with legs of <imath>2\sqrt5</imath> and base <imath>2\sqrt2</imath>. Then, the semi - perimeter of our triangle is, <cmath>\frac{4\sqrt5+2\sqrt2}{2} = 2\sqrt5 + \sqrt2.</cmath> Applying Heron's formula, we find that the area of this triangle is equivalent to <cmath>\sqrt{{(2\sqrt5+\sqrt2)}{(2\sqrt5-\sqrt2)}{(2)}} = \sqrt{{(20-2)}{(2)}} = \boxed{\textbf{(C) }6}.</cmath>

==Solution 12==
Like in the other solutions, we find that the three points of intersection are <imath>(2, 2)</imath>, <imath>(4, 6)</imath>, and <imath>(6, 4)</imath>. By the shoelace theorem, we have <cmath>\dfrac{1}{2} \left|(2*4 + 6*6 + 4*2) - (2*6 + 4*4 + 6*2) \right|</cmath> Evaluating this we get our answer of <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(C) }6}.</imath>
